source_text: Καὶ δοκεῖ μὲν ἀσαφὲς εἶναι τὸ εἰρημένον, γίνεται δὲ σαφέστερον διὰ τῶν ἑξῆς ἐπαγομένων· Καὶ γὰρ οἱ ὄντες ἐν τῷ σκήνει στενάζομεν βαρούμενοι, ἐφ' ᾧ οὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι. Ὁρᾷς πῶς ἑαυτοῦ οὐκ ἐπιλανθάνεται, οὐδὲ καλεῖ οἰκίαν τὸ σῶμα τοῦτο, ἀλλὰ σκῆνος πάλιν· Ἐφ' ᾧ οὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι; Ἐνταῦθα τοῖς τοῦ σώματος διαβάλλουσι τὴν φύσιν, καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς τῆς ἡμετέρας κατηγοροῦσι καιρίαν ἔδωκε πληγήν. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ εἶπεν, ὅτι στενάζομεν καὶ ἐκδύσασθαι οὐ βουλόμεθα, ἵνα μὴ νομίσῃς, ὅτι ὡς κακὸν φεύγει τὸ σῶμα καὶ πονηρίας αἴτιον καὶ ἐχθρὸν καὶ πολέμιον, ἄκουσον πῶς διορθοῦται τὴν ὑπόνοιαν· πρῶτον μὲν τῷ εἰπεῖν, ὅτι Στενάζομεν τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιποθοῦντες· ὁ γὰρ ἐπενδυόμενος τῷ ὄντι ἕτερον ἐπενδύεται· ἔπειτα τῷ εἰπεῖν, Στενάζομεν βαρούμενοι, ἐφ' ᾧ οὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιποθοῦντες. Ὃ δὲ λέγει τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν· Οὐ τὴν σάρκα ἀποθέσθαι βουλόμεθα, φησὶν, ἀλλὰ τὴν φθοράν· οὐ τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλὰ τὸν θάνατον. Ἄλλο σῶμα, καὶ ἄλλο θάνατος· ἄλλο σῶμα, καὶ ἄλλο φθορά· οὔτε τὸ σῶμα φθορὰ, οὔτε ἡ φθορὰ σῶμα. Καὶ φθαρτὸν μὲν τὸ σῶμα, οὐ φθορὰ δὲ τὸ σῶμα· καὶ θνητὸν μὲν τὸ σῶμα, οὐ θάνατος δὲ τὸ σῶμα· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν σῶμα ἔργον ἐγένετο τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἡ δὲ φθορὰ καὶ ὁ θάνατος ὑπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας εἰσήχθη. Τὸ γοῦν ἀλλότριον ἀποδύσασθαι βούλομαι, φησὶν, οὐ τὸ οἰκεῖον· ἀλλότριον δὲ, οὐ τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλ' ἡ φθορά. Διὰ τοῦτό φησιν· Ἐφ' ᾧ οὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, τουτέστι, τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι τῷ σώματι τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν. Μέσον ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα φθορᾶς καὶ ἀφθαρσίας. Ἀποδύεται τοίνυν φθορὰν, καὶ ἐπενδύεται ἀφθαρσίαν· ἀποβάλλει ὅπερ ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, καὶ κτᾶται ὅπερ ἔδωκεν ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ χάρις. Καὶ ἵνα μάθῃς, ὅτι τὸ ἐκδύσασθαι οὐ περὶ τοῦ σώματός φησιν, ἀλλὰ περὶ τῆς φθορᾶς καὶ τοῦ θανάτου, ἄκουσον τῶν ἐπαγομένων εὐθέως. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Οὐ θέλομεν ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι, οὐκ εἶπεν· Ἵνα καταποθῇ τὸ σῶμα ὑπὸ τῆς ἀσωματότητος· ἀλλὰ τί; Ἵνα καταποθῇ τὸ θνητὸν ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς, τουτέστιν, ἵνα ἀφανισθῆ, ἵνα ἀπόληται· ὥστε ἀπώλειαν οὐχὶ τοῦ σώματος λέγει, ἀλλὰ θανάτου καὶ φθορᾶς. Ἐπερχομένη γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ οὐχὶ τὸ σῶμα ἀφανίζει καὶ δαπανᾷ, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐπιγινομένην αὐτῷ φθορὰν καὶ τὸν θάνατον. Ὃ τοίνυν στεναγμὸς οὐ διὰ τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν ἐπικειμένην φθοράν· καὶ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα βαρύ ἐστι καὶ φορτικὸν καὶ ἐπαχθὲς, οὐ παρὰ τὴν οἰκείαν φύσιν, ἀλλὰ παρὰ τὴν ὕστερον αὐτῷ προσγενομένην θνητότητα. Ἀλλ' οὐχὶ σῶμα φθαρτὸν, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτόν ἐστι. Τοσαύτη γὰρ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν ἡ εὐγένεια, ὡς καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ φθορᾷ τὴν ἀξίαν ἐπιδείκνυσθαι τὴν αὑτοῦ. Αἱ γοῦν σκιαὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων τὰς ἀσωμάτους ἀπήλασαν δυνάμεις, καὶ ἡ κόνις καὶ ἡ τέφρα δαιμόνων περιεγένετο, καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια τὰ ὁμιλήσαντα τοῖς σώμασιν αὐτῶν νόσους ἀνεῖλον, καὶ ὑγίειαν ἐπανήγαγον. ζʹ. Μὴ γάρ μοι φλέγμα καὶ χολὴν εἴπῃς, καὶ ἱδρῶτα, καὶ ῥύπον, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα, ἅπερ οἱ κατηγοροῦντες τοῦ σώματος λέγουσιν· οὐ γὰρ τῆς τοῦ σώματος φύσεως ταῦτα ἦν, ἀλλὰ τῆς ὕστερον ἐπιγενομένης φθορᾶς.
thought_title: The body is not the enemy; corruption and death are
orientation: Chrysostom is expounding Paul's words in 2 Corinthians 5:2–4, defending the body against those who accuse its nature.
pass_a_gloss: And it seems [on the one hand] unclear to be the [thing] said, [but] it becomes clearer through the [things] next brought in: For indeed we the [ones] being in the tent groan being weighed down, on which [condition] not we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon. You see how of himself not he forgets, nor calls house this body, but tent again: On which [condition] not we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon? Here to the [ones] slandering the nature of the body, and accusing our flesh, a timely he gave blow. For since he said, that we groan and to be unclothed not we wish, in order that not you think, that as evil he flees the body and [as] cause of wickedness and enemy and hostile, hear how he corrects the suspicion: first [on the one hand] by the saying, that We groan our dwelling the [one] from heaven to be clothed upon longing; for the [one] being clothed upon in reality another [garment] is clothed upon; then by the saying, We groan being weighed down, on which [condition] not we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon longing. And what he says such is: Not the flesh to put off we wish, he says, but the corruption; not the body, but the death. One [thing] body, and another [thing] death; one [thing] body, and another [thing] corruption; neither the body corruption, nor the corruption body. And corruptible [on the one hand] the body, not corruption but the body; and mortal [on the one hand] the body, not death but the body; but the [on the one hand] body work became of God, the but corruption and the death by sin was brought in. The therefore alien [thing] to put off I wish, he says, not the own [thing]; alien but, not the body, but the corruption. Through this he says: On which [condition] not we wish to be unclothed, that is, the body, but to be clothed upon to the body the incorruption. Middle is the body of corruption and of incorruption. It puts off therefore corruption, and puts on incorruption; it casts off what it received from sin, and acquires what gave the grace of God. And in order that you learn, that the to be unclothed not about the body he says, but about the corruption and the death, hear the [things] brought in immediately. For having said, Not we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, not he said: In order that may be swallowed the body by the bodilessness; but what? In order that may be swallowed the mortal by the life, that is, in order that it may be made to disappear, in order that it may perish; so that destruction not of the body he speaks, but of death and of corruption. For coming upon [it] the life not the body makes disappear and consumes, but the [corruption] coming upon it and the death. The therefore groaning not because of the body, but because of the lying upon [it] corruption; for indeed the body heavy is and burdensome and oppressive, not because of [its] own nature, but because of the later to it added mortality. But not body corruptible, but incorruptible is. For so great of it is the nobility, as also in the corruption itself the worth to display its own. The therefore shadows of the apostles the bodiless drove away powers, and the dust and the ash over demons prevailed, and the garments the [ones] having associated with the bodies of them diseases removed, and health brought back. 7. Not for to me phlegm and bile may you speak, and sweat, and filth, and the other [things], which the [ones] accusing the body say; for not of the nature of the body these were, but of the later coming upon [it] corruption.

lemmas.gloss: to be clothed over, to put on over
to be stripped, to put off
may be swallowed up, may be consumed

choices.why: The prefix ἐπ- indicates putting on over something already present; Chrysostom contrasts it with stripping off, so the rendering must preserve the 'over' nuance.
The middle voice with the body as implied object; Chrysostom uses it to mean putting off the body, so 'stripped' keeps the force of removal.
καιρία πληγή is a mortal or well-aimed blow; 'decisive' captures the rhetorical force against the body's accusers.
The abstract noun formed from ἀσώματος; Chrysostom rejects the idea that the body is swallowed by bodilessness, so the abstract form is needed.
ἐπαχθής means heavy to bear, burdensome; 'oppressive' conveys the felt weight without implying moral fault.
Both nouns are articular and concrete; Chrysostom refers to relics of the apostles, so the literal pair is kept.

pass_b_english: The saying seems unclear at first, but it becomes clearer through what follows. For he says, “For while we are in this tent, we groan, being weighed down, because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over” (2 Corinthians 5:4). Do you see how he does not forget himself, and does not call this body a dwelling, but again a tent? “Because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over.” Here he gave a decisive blow to those who slander the nature of the body and accuse our flesh. Since he said that we groan and do not want to be stripped, so that you would not think he flees the body as something evil, a cause of wickedness, an enemy and adversary, hear how he corrects that suspicion. First, by saying, “We groan, longing to be clothed over with our dwelling place from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2). For the one who is clothed over puts on something else over what already exists. Then by saying, “We groan, being weighed down, because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over, longing for it.” What he means is this: We do not want to put off the flesh, he says, but corruption; not the body, but death. The body is one thing, and death is another. The body is one thing, and corruption is another. The body is not corruption, nor is corruption the body. The body is corruptible, but the body is not corruption. The body is mortal, but the body is not death. The body was made by God, but corruption and death were introduced by sin. So I want to strip off what is foreign, he says, not what is my own. And what is foreign is not the body, but corruption. That is why he says, “Because we do not want to be stripped”—that is, of the body—“but to be clothed over” with incorruption for the body. The body stands between corruption and incorruption. It strips off corruption and is clothed over with incorruption. It casts off what it received from sin, and acquires what the grace of God gave. And so that you may learn that when he says “to be stripped,” he is not speaking about the body but about corruption and death, listen to what follows immediately. After saying, “We do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over,” he did not say, “So that the body may be swallowed up by bodilessness.” But what? “So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4)—that is, so that it may be destroyed, so that it may perish. So he speaks of the destruction not of the body, but of death and corruption. For when life comes upon it, it does not destroy and consume the body, but the corruption and death that have come upon it. So the groaning is not because of the body, but because of the corruption that lies upon it. For the body is heavy, burdensome, and oppressive, not by its own nature, but because of the mortality that was added to it later. But the body is not corruptible; it is incorruptible. For its nobility is so great that even in corruption itself it displays its own dignity. The shadows of the apostles drove away bodiless powers, the dust and ashes prevailed over demons, and the garments that touched their bodies removed diseases and restored health.
Do not tell me about phlegm and bile, sweat and filth, and the other things the accusers of the body mention. These were not part of the body's nature, but of the corruption that came upon it later.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'bodiless powers' but context is about apostles' shadows defeating them; 'powers' alone loses the contrast with bodily dignity.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Powers' translates δυνάμεις; 'bodiless' renders ἀσωμάτους. Accurate, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: But the body is not corruptible; it is incorruptible.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἀλλ' οὐχὶ σῶμα φθαρτὸν, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτόν ἐστι.
last_rejected.why: Greek says body is corruptible but becomes incorruptible, not that it already is.
last_rejected.fix: But the body is not merely corruptible; it becomes incorruptible.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτόν ἐστι = 'but it IS incorruptible.' Translation correctly renders present indicative; no tense change implied.

last_rejected.quote: the body is heavy, burdensome, and oppressive
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ σῶμα βαρύ ἐστι καὶ φορτικὸν καὶ ἐπαχθὲς
last_rejected.why: Greek says body IS heavy/burdensome now, not that it is oppressive in a moral sense.
last_rejected.fix: the body is heavy, burdensome, and weighed down
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπαχθὲς means burdensome/oppressive; 'oppressive' is within normal range. No meaning change.
